meta.theme: the ethics of nudging: the complaint about influence proves too much because no arrangement is neutral, so the objection should be narrowed to influence that works only while the chooser is unaware of it

source.usage_note: Original composition in CAT register for CAT OS; no external source adapted. Personal study only.

meta.prompt_version: content engine v1 (content/taxonomy/AUTHORING.md); batch-rc-003, task rc-02
meta.reviewer_notes: A long passage written at foundation difficulty: short sentences, concrete examples, a signposted five-step argument. The work is in the last paragraph, which limits the test the fourth paragraph has just proposed, and which most of the harder options are built to catch readers who stopped before it.

quality.adversarial_review: Every hard option in this set is built from a reader who stopped at the end of the fourth paragraph. Q3's rival says an arrangement surviving disclosure must be aimed at the chooser's good; the fifth paragraph denies it in one sentence, allowing an honest arrangement aimed at something harmful. Q4's rival is that passing the test shows an arrangement worth adopting, the same slide from a necessary test to a sufficient one. Q5's rival is triumphant, which would be right if the paragraph did not exist, and the paragraph exists in order to mark two limits. Q6's rival is the option that objections to nudging have no force, which is the second paragraph's premise promoted to the conclusion; the passage uses it only to say the objection has been badly aimed, and then re-aims it. Q1's rival is the claim that people cannot predict what any individual will choose, which is true of the world and irrelevant to why the complaint fails.

paragraphs.text: Choices arrive arranged. The salad sits at the front of the counter and the chips at the back. The form has a box already ticked. The letter from the surgery mentions that most people in your street have had the injection. None of these things forbids you anything, and each of them changes what a good many people do. Arrangements of this kind are now standard equipment in government and in business, and they have a name: nudges. The objection to them is easy to state and widely felt. Somebody has worked out how you make decisions and is using that knowledge to steer you, without asking your permission and usually without your noticing.

The objection as stated cannot be right, because it proves too much. Somebody has to decide what goes at the front of the counter. If the chips go there instead, that is also an arrangement, and it also changes what people do. If every box on the form is left empty, that is a third arrangement, with effects of its own, and it is not the absence of one. There is no neutral canteen and no neutral form. Since every possible version of a choice influences the choice, the complaint that you have been influenced cannot pick out the arrangements people actually object to. It catches all of them equally, which means it distinguishes nothing.

So the objection needs sharpening, and it is not hard to see where the sharp edge lies. What people resent is not being influenced. It is being influenced in a way that depends on their not knowing. Notice that the question is not whether the chooser would approve of the arrangement; plenty of people disapprove of things that are good for them, and approval is a poor test of anything. The question is narrower and much easier to apply. Suppose the whole thing were explained to the person being nudged, in plain words, at the moment of the choice. Some arrangements would carry on working exactly as before. Others would collapse the instant they were described. That difference is not a small one, and it turns out to be the difference people have been trying to name all along.

Take the counter first. Put a sign above it: the salad is at the front because people take what they see first, so have whatever you want. Nothing has been hidden and nobody has been tricked, and a good many people will still take the salad, because seeing a thing first really does make it easier to take. Now take a page on a website built so that cancelling a subscription requires four screens and an unmarked button. Put up the corresponding sign: this page has been made difficult so that you will give up. Nobody gives up. The page has no effect that survives being described, which is another way of saying that it never had an effect of its own at all. It borrowed one from your ignorance and gave it back the moment the ignorance ended.

The test is worth having and it is not a licence. It answers one question, whether an arrangement is manipulating the person it acts on, and it is silent about a second, whether the thing people are being steered towards is any good for them. An arrangement can be announced with perfect honesty and still push a chooser towards something that harms him, and announcing it does not improve matters in the least. There is an awkward middle as well. Some genuinely helpful arrangements probably lose part of their force when they are described, without depending on secrecy altogether, and about those the test says only that they are the hard cases. It is a first question rather than a last one. That is what a good first question usually is.

questions.target_mistake: answering with a true remark about nudges instead of the reason the passage actually gives for rejecting the complaint about influence
questions.stem: According to the passage, the complaint that a nudge has influenced your choice fails because

options.A: every possible arrangement of a choice, including leaving it exactly as it is, influences the choice
options.B: people who have an arrangement explained to them usually end up approving of it
options.C: the person arranging a choice cannot know in advance which option any single individual will take in the end
options.D: influence counts as manipulation only when the party arranging the choice is a government

explanation.expert_notice: The second paragraph gives the reason and then repeats it in three forms: putting the chips at the front is also an arrangement, leaving every box empty is a third arrangement and not the absence of one, and there is no neutral canteen and no neutral form. The paragraph ends by drawing the consequence itself.
explanation.correct_reasoning: The correct option is that consequence. If there is no version of the counter or the form that fails to influence people, then pointing at influence cannot separate the arrangements anybody objects to from the arrangements nobody would. The passage puts it exactly so: the complaint catches all of them equally, which means it distinguishes nothing.
explanation.question_type_note: A detail question about why an argument fails is answered from the sentence that states the failure, not from any true statement about the subject.
explanation.reading_habit: When an author says an objection proves too much, look for the sentence naming what else it would catch. That sentence is the reason, and questions are set on it.

distractors.why_wrong: The passage says the opposite about approval, and says it directly: plenty of people disapprove of things that are good for them, and approval is a poor test of anything.
distractors.seductive_element: The whole argument turns on explaining an arrangement to the chooser, so approval after explanation feels like the point being made.

distractors.why_wrong: Nothing in the passage depends on predicting individuals; the examples are all about what a good many people do, and the complaint is rejected because no arrangement can avoid influencing them.
distractors.seductive_element: It is plainly true of real nudges and sounds like a sensible limit on how much power an arranger has.

distractors.why_wrong: The passage treats government and business alike, naming both in its first paragraph and using a commercial website for its clearest example of an arrangement that fails the test.
distractors.seductive_element: Public suspicion of nudging is loudest when the state is doing it, so restricting the charge to governments sounds like the familiar version of the worry.

questions.target_mistake: reading a case chosen to make a test visible as a complaint about the people or the industry that supplied it
questions.prediction_target: The learner should be able to say beforehand: this example is the one that dies when it is announced, and it is there to show the other half of the test.
questions.stem: The author describes a web page built so that cancelling a subscription takes four screens and an unmarked button chiefly in order to

options.A: show that private companies behave worse than governments do
options.B: give a case in which announcing how the arrangement works would destroy its effect
options.C: illustrate how common such designs have become on the internet
options.D: suggest that people give up too easily whenever a task is made difficult

explanation.expert_notice: The example arrives in a paragraph with two halves and an explicit instruction for each: put a sign above the counter, then put up the corresponding sign on the page. One arrangement keeps working with the sign in place and the other does not, and the sentence after the example says what that shows.
explanation.correct_reasoning: The correct option names the job the case is doing. The counter supplies the half of the test that survives disclosure; the cancellation page supplies the half that collapses, and the passage draws the conclusion at once by saying the page never had an effect of its own and borrowed one from the reader's ignorance. Remove the example and the test has only one side.
explanation.question_type_note: A role-of-detail question asks what a particular is for. Find the claim on either side of it, since an author usually says what a detail has just established.
explanation.reading_habit: When examples come in pairs, ask what differs between them. The difference is almost always the thing the author is trying to make visible, and it is what the question will be about.

distractors.why_wrong: No comparison between business and government is drawn anywhere; the first paragraph puts them together as users of the same equipment, and the argument is about arrangements rather than about who makes them.
distractors.seductive_element: The unflattering example happens to be commercial and the flattering one happens to be a canteen, which invites a contrast the passage never makes.

distractors.why_wrong: Nothing is said about how common such pages are. The example is chosen for a property it has, namely that it cannot survive being described, not for how often it occurs.
distractors.seductive_element: Readers meet such pages constantly, so the example reads as a complaint about their spread rather than as a test case.

distractors.why_wrong: That people give up is the mechanism the page exploits, not a criticism the passage is making of them; the criticism falls on an arrangement that works only while its purpose is concealed.
distractors.seductive_element: Giving up really is what happens in the example, and the passage does say so in as many words.

questions.target_mistake: treating a test that clears an arrangement of manipulation as a verdict that the arrangement is good
questions.prediction_target: The learner should predict that surviving disclosure settles only the manipulation question, because the last paragraph says the test is silent about whether the destination is any good.
questions.stem: It can be inferred from the passage that an arrangement which goes on working after it has been fully explained

options.A: must be aimed at something that is good for the chooser himself
options.B: is one that no chooser anywhere would have any reason to object to
options.C: does not in fact influence the chooser's decision in any way
options.D: has passed the author's test, which still leaves open whether it ought to be used

explanation.expert_notice: The last paragraph does two things and says so: the test answers one question, whether an arrangement manipulates, and is silent about a second, whether what people are being steered towards is good for them. It then supplies the case that proves the silence, an honest arrangement pushing someone towards harm.
explanation.correct_reasoning: Surviving disclosure is exactly what the test measures, so an arrangement that does survive has passed it. What the passage refuses to add is any conclusion about the destination, which is why it says announcing an arrangement does not improve matters in the least when the arrangement points somewhere bad. The correct option grants the pass and withholds the verdict, which is the author's own position.
explanation.question_type_note: When an author proposes a test and then limits it, inference questions ask you to keep the limit. The strongest wrong answers are the ones that would be right if the limiting paragraph did not exist.
explanation.reading_habit: Whenever a passage offers a test, ask what the test does not measure. Authors who are worth reading say so, usually in the paragraph after the test is introduced, and that sentence is where most of the questions live.

distractors.why_wrong: The final paragraph denies precisely this, allowing an arrangement that is announced with perfect honesty and still pushes a chooser towards something that harms him.
distractors.seductive_element: The two examples in the passage happen to line up, a wholesome one that survives disclosure and a shabby one that does not, which suggests the test tracks goodness.

distractors.why_wrong: The passage rules approval out as a test in the third paragraph, remarking that plenty of people disapprove of things that are good for them, so nothing follows about what every chooser would accept.
distractors.seductive_element: An arrangement that works even after being explained sounds like one nobody could reasonably mind.

distractors.why_wrong: The point of the surviving case is that it does influence people and carries on doing so in the open; the passage explains why, since seeing a thing first really does make it easier to take.
distractors.seductive_element: Disclosure is expected to neutralise influence, so an arrangement that is permissible after disclosure can seem to be one that no longer works.

questions.target_mistake: collapsing the passage's two questions into one, so that passing the first counts as an answer to the second
questions.prediction_target: The learner should be able to say: the paragraph splits the judgement in two and hands the test only the first half.
questions.stem: Which of the following follows from the final paragraph?

options.A: An arrangement that passes the test is thereby shown to be worth adopting.
options.B: An arrangement that is aimed at a bad end will always turn out to fail the test sooner or later.
options.C: Two separate questions have to be asked about a nudge, and the test answers only the first.
options.D: The test should be abandoned, since it cannot settle the cases that matter most.

explanation.expert_notice: The paragraph is built on the word one and the word second. It answers one question, whether the arrangement manipulates, and it is silent about a second, whether the destination is good. The closing lines then put the same structure in another way by calling it a first question rather than a last one.
explanation.correct_reasoning: The implication is a division of labour. Deciding what to think of a nudge takes two judgements, and the author has supplied a method for one of them while saying plainly that the other is untouched. The correct option states the division without adding a verdict about either half, which is as far as the paragraph goes.
explanation.question_type_note: An implication question wants what the text commits its author to, not what it says. Where a paragraph separates two questions, the implication is usually the separation itself.
explanation.reading_habit: Count the questions an author says he is answering. When the number is smaller than the number the topic requires, the missing one is where the implication questions are set.

distractors.why_wrong: The paragraph exists to block this step, allowing an arrangement that is announced with perfect honesty and still harms the chooser; passing the test clears an arrangement of one charge and recommends nothing.
distractors.seductive_element: A test proposed at length in the previous paragraph feels as if it must deliver a verdict, and this is the verdict a reader expects it to deliver.

distractors.why_wrong: The passage supplies the counter-example itself. An arrangement pointed at something harmful may be described honestly and go on working, which is why the author has to introduce a second question at all.
distractors.seductive_element: The one arrangement in the passage that fails the test is also the shabbiest, which makes a rule out of a coincidence between two examples.

distractors.why_wrong: The paragraph opens by calling the test worth having and closes by calling it a good first question; the hard middle cases are named as its limit, not as grounds for discarding it.
distractors.seductive_element: A paragraph spent listing what a method cannot do reads as a retraction if the opening and closing sentences are skimmed.

questions.target_mistake: expecting a closing paragraph to celebrate the proposal that precedes it, and so missing that this one is spent marking limits
questions.prediction_target: The learner should be able to say: the closing paragraph is the author taking something away from his own idea, calmly and on purpose.
questions.stem: The tone of the final paragraph is best described as

options.A: careful, limiting the value of the author's own proposal
options.B: apologetic, implying that the test was a mistake to propose
options.C: triumphant, offering the test as the answer to the whole problem
options.D: detached, reporting what others say about nudging without judging it

explanation.expert_notice: The paragraph begins by giving with one hand and taking with the other: the test is worth having and it is not a licence. Everything after that sentence names a boundary, and the last two sentences find a positive way of stating the same limit by calling it a first question rather than a last one.
explanation.correct_reasoning: Two limits are set out in order, one about what the test cannot judge and one about cases it can only classify as hard, and both are stated without embarrassment or retreat. That is care: an author checking his own proposal before a reader has to, and keeping it while saying exactly how far it reaches.
explanation.question_type_note: Tone questions are decided by what a paragraph does, not by whether its sentences sound warm or cold. A paragraph spent on limits is careful; a paragraph spent on defending is something else.
explanation.reading_habit: Read a closing paragraph for direction as well as feeling. If it reduces what the passage has just claimed, the author is being careful, and an option that makes him either regretful or victorious has misread the movement.

distractors.why_wrong: Nothing is withdrawn. The paragraph opens by calling the test worth having and closes by saying that a good first question is exactly what this is, which is a defence of the proposal rather than an apology for it.
distractors.seductive_element: A paragraph listing what an idea cannot do sounds like a retreat if only the middle of it is read.

distractors.why_wrong: The paragraph exists in order to deny that the test settles everything, naming a question it is silent about and a set of cases it can only call hard.
distractors.seductive_element: The preceding paragraph ends on a genuinely satisfying example, and a reader carries the satisfaction forward into a paragraph that is doing the opposite.

distractors.why_wrong: The passage's voice here is entirely the author's own: he calls the test worth having, denies it is a licence, and judges an honestly announced but harmful arrangement to be no better for the honesty.
distractors.seductive_element: The paragraph is measured and quiet, and measured prose is easily mistaken for the absence of a position.

questions.target_mistake: taking the second paragraph's premise, that no arrangement is neutral, for the passage's conclusion about nudging
questions.prediction_target: The learner should be able to say: the objection is not dropped but re-aimed, from influence as such to influence that needs the chooser's ignorance.
questions.stem: Which of the following best captures the main idea of the passage?

options.A: Nudging is a form of manipulation, because it works on people without their agreement.
options.B: Since there is no neutral way to present a choice, objections to nudging have no force.
options.C: Deliberately confusing cancellation pages ought to be banned, and helpful defaults ought to be actively encouraged instead.
options.D: What matters is not influence, which is unavoidable, but influence that works only while the chooser is unaware of it.

explanation.expert_notice: The passage has a shape it announces as it goes: an objection, a demonstration that the objection proves too much, a sharpening, a test with two worked cases, and then two limits on the test. The sharpening is where the thesis lives, and the third paragraph says so, calling it the difference people have been trying to name all along.
explanation.correct_reasoning: The correct option is that sharpened objection. Influence is conceded to be unavoidable, which is the second paragraph's work, and the complaint is then re-aimed at arrangements that depend on the chooser not knowing, which is what the fourth paragraph's pair of examples demonstrates. It keeps both halves and adds neither a ban nor a blessing.
explanation.question_type_note: In a problem and prescription passage the main idea is the reformulated problem together with its test, not the step used to clear the ground.
explanation.reading_habit: When an author shows that an objection proves too much, expect him to rebuild it rather than abandon it. The rebuilt version is the thesis, and the sentence introducing it usually contains a word like narrower or sharper.

distractors.why_wrong: This is the objection as the first paragraph states it, and the second paragraph answers it at once by showing that it condemns every possible arrangement, including doing nothing.
distractors.seductive_element: It is stated first, stated sympathetically, and described as widely felt, which reads as endorsement.

distractors.why_wrong: It takes the passage's own sentence, that there is no neutral canteen and no neutral form, and turns a premise into a verdict. The second paragraph uses that fact to show that one version of the objection fails, and the three paragraphs after it build a version that works.
distractors.seductive_element: It is the live rival, since the premise it states is one the passage argues for at length, and a reader who stops there has been given no conclusion yet.

distractors.why_wrong: No rule is proposed for anyone to enforce. The passage supplies a way of telling two kinds of arrangement apart and then says explicitly that passing the test settles only one of the two questions that matter.
distractors.seductive_element: The two examples are so clearly contrasted that they read as a policy with a good side and a bad side already marked out.

vocabulary.passage_use: There is no neutral canteen and no neutral form
vocabulary.meaning_here: taking no side and producing no effect of its own

vocabulary.passage_use: What people resent is not being influenced
vocabulary.meaning_here: feel wronged by, and hold against whoever did it

vocabulary.passage_use: It borrowed one from your ignorance
vocabulary.meaning_here: took from somewhere else rather than possessing in its own right

mentor.challenge: A simple argument in five clear steps, with the real work in the last one. Read to the end before deciding what the author thinks his test proves.
mentor.one_sentence_summary: Complaining that a nudge influenced you proves too much, because every arrangement of a choice influences it, so the objection should be re-aimed at arrangements that stop working the moment they are explained — a test which shows when influence is manipulation and says nothing about whether the destination is good.
mentor.main_idea: Every way of presenting a choice affects what people do, so influence cannot be the complaint. What people actually object to is influence that needs them not to know about it. Ask what would happen if the arrangement were explained at the moment of choosing: some survive and some collapse. That test separates the two kinds and answers only one of the two questions worth asking.
mentor.simple_explanation:
Choices come pre-arranged. The salad is in front, the chips are behind. A box on the form is already ticked. A letter tells you that most of your neighbours have had the injection. Nothing is forbidden, and yet more people take the salad and tick the box.

The usual complaint is that someone is steering you without permission. The author says that complaint cannot be right, because it would catch everything. Someone has to decide what goes in front. Putting the chips there is a decision too. Leaving every box empty is a decision too, and it changes what people do as well. There is no arrangement that has no effect, so saying 'you influenced me' does not single out anything.

So what do people actually mind? Being influenced in a way that needs them not to know. Here is the test. Imagine the arrangement is explained to you, in plain words, right when you are choosing. Does it still work?

Try it on the salad. Put a sign up: 'The salad is at the front because people take what they see first. Have whatever you like.' Plenty of people still take the salad, because what you see first really is easier to take. Nothing was hidden, and nothing collapses.

Now try it on a website that makes cancelling your subscription take four screens and a button nobody can find. Put up the matching sign: 'This page is deliberately hard so that you give up.' Nobody gives up. The design never had a power of its own. It borrowed one from you not knowing, and it hands that power straight back.

Finally, the author is careful about what his test does. It tells you whether you are being manipulated. It does not tell you whether the thing you are being pushed towards is good for you. Someone can be perfectly open about steering you somewhere harmful, and being open does not fix that. And some genuinely useful arrangements probably weaken a bit when explained without relying on secrecy, so those stay difficult. The test is a good first question, not the last one.
mentor.why_difficult: The sentences are easy and the structure is not. The argument reaches what looks like a conclusion twice before it reaches its actual one: first when the complaint about influence is knocked down, which readers mistake for a defence of nudging, and again when the test is demonstrated, which readers mistake for a full verdict. The last paragraph then withdraws half of what the test seemed to promise, and most of the wrong answers in this set would be correct if that paragraph did not exist.
mentor.author_intention: To rescue a widely felt objection from the bad version of itself, by showing what the objection was really about and giving the reader a question he can actually ask.

paragraph_journey.note: Choices come already arranged, and arrangements change what people do without forbidding anything. The usual objection is that this is steering without permission.
Every possible arrangement influences people, including leaving things alone. So complaining about influence catches everything and singles out nothing.
What people mind is influence that needs them not to know. The test is not whether they would approve but whether the arrangement survives being explained.
A sign over the salad changes nothing; people still take it. A sign on the cancellation page destroys it, because its only power came from your not knowing.
It says whether you are being manipulated, not whether the destination is good. Some helpful arrangements weaken when announced, and those stay hard. It is a first question.

mentor.tone_progression: Brisk and illustrative at the start, mildly impatient with the loose version of the objection, confident while the test is demonstrated, and then deliberately careful at the close, where the author marks the boundaries of his own proposal.
key_transitions: 'The objection as stated cannot be right, because it proves too much.' (opening of paragraph 2) — the complaint is taken apart before it is rebuilt.
'What people resent is not being influenced. It is being influenced in a way that depends on their not knowing.' (paragraph 3) — the objection is re-aimed, and this is the thesis.
'The test is worth having and it is not a licence.' (opening of paragraph 5) — the proposal is kept and cut down to size in the same sentence.
mentor.misunderstanding: Two wrong pictures are common. The first is that the author defends nudging, because he spends a paragraph demolishing the complaint against it; in fact he demolishes one version in order to build a better one. The second, and the one this set punishes hardest, is that passing the test makes an arrangement acceptable. The last paragraph says an arrangement can be announced with perfect honesty and still push someone towards harm, so a pass clears one charge and settles nothing else.
mentor.traps_summary: The options here do three things again and again. They offer the opening complaint as the author's own view. They stop at the second paragraph and turn its premise, that nothing is neutral, into a conclusion that objections are pointless. And they treat the test as sufficient when the author has been at pains to call it a first question.
mentor.reading_lesson: When an author gives you a test, immediately ask two things: what does it decide, and what does it leave undecided. Good writers answer both, usually in the paragraph straight after the test is demonstrated, and that paragraph is where the questions cluster. Readers who stop at the demonstration have the method without its limits, which is exactly the position every distractor in a passage of this shape is designed for.
mentor.real_world: You can run the test yourself this week, on a queue that has been laid out to keep you walking past the sweets, a subscription that renews unless you act, or an email whose unsubscribe link is a pale grey. Ask what would happen if the designer put up a sign explaining the plan.
mentor.takeaway: Influence you could be told about is not manipulation; influence that dies when it is described never had any strength of its own.
mentor.reflection_question: Which of the arrangements you meet every day would still work if somebody put up a sign explaining exactly how they work?
